hook: For decades, memory decline was considered inevitable... That belief changed with the discovery of Alpha-GPC.
claim: Brain Memory Keeper is a memory and focus supplement built around Alpha-GPC, a choline compound the brain uses to make the neurotransmitter acetylcholine. The seller recommends a six-month course followed by a lower 'maintenance' dose.
ing_note: The website lists ginkgo leaf extract standardized to 24% (the same standard used in most ginkgo studies) and St. John's Wort at 0.3% hypericin, but does not give milligram amounts for the blend.
use: One capsule a day, usually after breakfast, according to the seller. The seller suggests six months of daily use, then 'a few capsules per week'.
price_note: A smaller starter package is also offered at $79 plus $9.99 shipping.
bonuses: A free bonus book with the 3-bottle package
Two free bonuses with the 6-bottle package
checks: Alpha-GPC, bacopa, ginkgo and phosphatidylserine all have some human research for memory, but results are modest and depend on doses the label doesn't confirm.
Large trials (such as the GEM study of ginkgo in older adults) found no protection against dementia.
St. John's Wort is an unusual addition for memory and causes serious drug interactions.
The references cited include rat studies and news articles rather than trials of this product.
pros: Uses ingredients with real memory research behind them
cons: No milligram amounts for the blend
St. John's Wort interacts with many common medicines
Recommends long use before judging results
verdict: Brain Memory Keeper is more transparent than most memory supplements and uses ingredients with genuine, if modest, research. The big caveat is St. John's Wort: anyone on antidepressants, birth control, blood thinners, heart or transplant medicines should not take it without medical advice. Sudden or worsening memory problems should always be checked by a doctor.
